electromagnetic-spectrum-s1.title: Infrared spectrum of an unknown liquid
electromagnetic-spectrum-s1.text: The percent of infrared light transmitted through an unknown liquid. Dips show wavenumbers that are absorbed. Typical absorptions: O–H stretch 3,200–3,550 cm⁻¹ (broad); C–H stretch 2,850–3,000 cm⁻¹; C=O stretch 1,680–1,750 cm⁻¹; C–O stretch 1,000–1,300 cm⁻¹. Higher wavenumber means higher energy.

electromagnetic-spectrum-s2.title: Visible absorption of a dye solution
electromagnetic-spectrum-s2.text: How strongly a dye solution absorbs light across the visible spectrum, on a relative scale where higher means more light of that wavelength is absorbed. Colors: violet 400–450 nm, blue 450–495, green 495–570, yellow 570–590, orange 590–620, red 620–700 nm.

items.q: What happens in the molecules when they absorb the light at about 3,350 cm⁻¹?
options: An O–H bond vibrates more strongly.
An electron moves to a higher energy level.
The molecule rotates faster.
An inner electron is removed.

why.correct: Infrared photons match the energy gaps between vibrational levels. The broad dip near 3,350 cm⁻¹ is in the O–H stretch range.
options: Right: IR excites vibrations; this one is O–H.
Electronic transitions need visible or UV photons, which carry more energy.
Rotation is changed by lower-energy microwaves.
Removing core electrons needs X-ray photons.

items.q: Which compound is the unknown most likely to be?
options: Ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH
Acetone, (CH₃)₂C=O
Hexane, C₆H₁₄
Water, H₂O

why.correct: The spectrum shows O–H (about 3,350), C–H (about 2,950) and C–O (about 1,050 cm⁻¹) absorptions, and no C=O near 1,700. Ethanol has all three bonds and no C=O.
options: Right: O–H, C–H and C–O, no C=O.
Acetone would show a strong C=O dip near 1,700 cm⁻¹, which is missing.
Hexane has no O–H or C–O bonds, so it would lack the dips at 3,350 and 1,050 cm⁻¹.
Water has no C–H bonds, so it would lack the dip near 2,950 cm⁻¹.

items.q: The O–H absorption is at a higher wavenumber than the C–O absorption. What does this tell you?
options: Exciting the O–H vibration needs a higher-energy photon than exciting the C–O vibration.
The O–H bond absorbs more light than the C–O bond, because the dip is deeper.
The O–H bond vibrates more slowly than the C–O bond, because it is a lighter bond.
The O–H absorption moves an electron, while the C–O absorption moves the whole molecule.

why.correct: Higher wavenumber means more energy per photon. So the gap between O–H vibrational levels is larger than the gap between C–O vibrational levels.
options: Right: higher wavenumber, larger energy gap.
The position, not the depth, gives the energy.
A higher energy gap means a faster, not slower, vibration.
Both are infrared absorptions, so both are vibrations.

items.q: A sample of acetone is run on the same instrument. Which change would you expect in its spectrum compared with the unknown?
options: A new strong dip near 1,700 cm⁻¹ and no broad dip near 3,350 cm⁻¹.
The same spectrum, because both liquids contain carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.
No dips, because acetone is a polar molecule and so it does not absorb infrared.
A dip in the visible region, because acetone is a colored liquid.

why.correct: Acetone has a C=O bond (absorbs near 1,700 cm⁻¹) but no O–H bond, so the broad 3,350 cm⁻¹ dip disappears. IR spectra depend on the bonds, not only the elements.
options: Right: C=O appears; O–H disappears.
Different bonds give different absorptions even with the same elements.
Polar molecules absorb IR strongly.
Acetone is colorless; the instrument measures infrared here.

items.q: At which wavelength does the dye absorb most strongly?
options: About 630 nm
About 450 nm
About 540 nm
About 700 nm

why.correct: The absorption peaks near 630 nm, in the red-orange part of the spectrum.
options: Right: the peak of the curve.
Absorption there is close to zero.
Absorption there is low.
Absorption has fallen far from its peak by 700 nm.

items.q: What color does the dye solution appear?
options: Blue, because it absorbs red-orange light.
Red, because it absorbs red light most strongly.
Black, because it absorbs light across the visible spectrum.
Colorless, because it absorbs just one narrow band.

why.correct: We see the light that is not absorbed. Absorbing red-orange light near 630 nm leaves mostly blue and violet light to pass through, so the solution looks blue.
options: Right: the transmitted light sets the color.
A substance shows the color it does not absorb.
It absorbs little below 550 nm.
Absorbing a strong band of visible light gives a color.

items.q: What happens to a dye molecule when it absorbs a 630 nm photon?
options: An electron moves from a lower energy level to a higher one.
A bond in the molecule vibrates with more energy.
The molecule rotates faster about its center.
A covalent bond breaks and the molecule falls apart.

why.correct: Visible photons carry enough energy to match electronic energy gaps, so an electron is promoted to an excited state.
options: Right: an electronic transition.
Vibrations are excited by lower-energy infrared light.
Rotation is excited by microwaves.
Visible light excites the electron; the molecule stays intact.

items.q: Would shining 1,500 nm light on the dye cause the same electronic transition? Why?
options: No: a 1,500 nm photon carries less energy than the gap.
Yes: a longer wavelength carries more energy, which is more than enough for the gap.
Yes: any photon is absorbed once the light is bright enough, whatever its wavelength.
No: 1,500 nm light is an X-ray, which removes inner electrons instead.

why.correct: 1,500 nm is infrared, longer than 630 nm, so each photon has less energy. Absorption needs a photon whose energy matches the gap; more photons of the wrong energy do not add up.
options: Right: energy must match the gap.
Longer wavelength means lower energy per photon.
Each photon must match the gap on its own; brightness adds photons, not energy per photon.
1,500 nm is infrared, not X-ray.

items.q: Put these regions in order of increasing energy per photon.
options: Radio waves
Microwaves
Infrared
Visible light
Ultraviolet
X-rays

why.correct: Energy per photon rises as wavelength shrinks: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray.

items.q: Which pairings of a type of radiation with the change it causes in a molecule are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Microwave: faster rotation
Infrared: more bond vibration
Ultraviolet: faster rotation
Visible: more bond vibration
Ultraviolet: electrons promoted to higher levels
Radio: inner electrons removed

why.correct: Microwaves match rotational gaps, infrared vibrational gaps, and visible or ultraviolet light electronic gaps.
options: Right: microwaves match rotational gaps.
Right: infrared matches vibrational gaps.
UV photons carry far more energy than rotational gaps; they cause electronic transitions.
Visible light causes electronic transitions, not vibrations.
Right: UV matches electronic gaps.
Radio photons carry the least energy; removing core electrons needs X-rays.

items.q: Why does a microwave oven heat water but leave a dry glass plate fairly cool?
options: Microwaves make polar water molecules rotate faster, warming the food.
Microwaves carry more energy per photon than visible light, so they break the bonds in water.
Microwaves promote electrons in water to excited states, which give off heat as they return.
Microwaves make the glass vibrate, and the glass passes the heat to the water molecules in the food.

why.correct: Microwave photons match the energy gaps of molecular rotation. Polar water molecules absorb them, rotate faster, and collide with neighbors, raising the temperature. The glass absorbs little.
options: Right: rotation of polar molecules.
Microwave photons carry less energy than visible photons and break no bonds.
Electronic transitions need visible or UV photons.
The glass absorbs little microwave energy and is warmed by the food instead.

items.q: Which kind of radiation has the longest wavelength?
options: Microwave
Infrared
Visible
Ultraviolet

why.correct: Of these, microwaves have the longest wavelengths (1 mm to 1 m) and the lowest energy per photon.
options: Right: 1 mm to 1 m.
Infrared wavelengths are shorter than microwaves.
Visible light is 400–700 nm.
Ultraviolet is shorter than visible.

items.q: Ultraviolet light can damage skin cells, but infrared light from a heat lamp of the same brightness does not. Which explanation fits?
options: Each UV photon carries enough energy to excite electrons; an IR photon does not.
UV light is hotter than IR light, so it raises the skin's temperature more quickly.
IR light is absorbed by air before it reaches the skin, so very little arrives.
UV light has a longer wavelength, so it reaches deeper into the skin's cells.

why.correct: What matters is energy per photon. UV photons can promote electrons in molecules such as DNA and trigger reactions; IR photons only make bonds vibrate.
options: Right: energy per photon.
Light is not "hot"; heating comes from absorbed energy, and IR heats well.
IR from a heat lamp clearly reaches and warms the skin.
UV has a shorter wavelength than IR.

items.q: Nitrogen, N₂, makes up 78% of the air but is not a greenhouse gas, while CO₂ absorbs infrared strongly. Which claim is consistent with this?
options: N₂'s vibration does not absorb infrared; CO₂ has vibrations that do.
N₂ absorbs infrared more strongly than CO₂ but is too common to matter.
N₂ absorbs ultraviolet light, so it holds the most heat in the atmosphere.
CO₂ absorbs infrared because its electrons jump to higher energy levels.

why.correct: A vibration absorbs infrared only if it changes the molecule's charge distribution. N₂'s symmetric stretch does not; CO₂ has bending and uneven stretching vibrations that do.
options: Right: N₂ does not absorb IR.
N₂ does not absorb IR, so its abundance does not make it a greenhouse gas.
Absorbing UV is not what traps heat radiated from Earth's surface.
IR causes vibrations, not electronic transitions.

items.q: A molecule's two lowest electronic levels are far apart, but its vibrational levels are close together. Which light could it absorb to excite a vibration but not an electronic transition?
options: Infrared
Ultraviolet
Visible
X-ray

why.correct: Infrared photons have energies that match vibrational gaps but fall far short of electronic gaps.
options: Right: IR matches vibrational gaps.
UV photons match electronic gaps.
Visible photons match electronic gaps in colored substances.
X-ray photons remove inner electrons.
